COBS 19.1 Pension transfers, conversions, and opt-outs

COBS 19.1.-1A (01/10/2020, R): Except where a firm is providing abridged advice (see COBS 19.1A), this section applies to a firm which: (1) gives advice on pension transfers, pension conversions and pension opt-outs to a retail client; or (2) arranges pension transfers, pension conversions or pension opt-outs, in relation to: (3) a pension transfer; (4) a pension conversion; or (5) a pension opt-out from a scheme with safeguarded benefits or potential safeguarded benefits.

COBS 19.1.1A (01/04/2018, R): (1) A firm must ensure that advice on pension transfers, pension conversions and pension opt-outs is given or checked by a pension transfer specialist. (2) The requirement in (1) does not apply where the only safeguarded benefit involved is a guaranteed annuity rate.

COBS 19.1.1C (01/10/2020, R): (1) A firm must make a personal recommendation when it provides advice on conversion or transfer of pension benefits. (2) Before making the personal recommendation the firm must: (a) determine the proposed arrangement with flexible benefits to which the retail client would move; and (b) carry out the appropriate pension transfer analysis and produce the transfer value comparator. (3) The requirement in (2)(b) does not apply if the only safeguarded benefit involved is a guaranteed annuity rate. (4) The firm must take reasonable steps to ensure that the retail client understands how the key outcomes from the appropriate pension transfer analysis and the transfer value comparator contribute towards the personal recommendation. (5) Prior to making a personal recommendation to effect a pension transfer or pension conversion, a firm must obtain evidence that the client can demonstrate that they understand the risks to them of proceeding with the pension transfer or pension conversion.

COBS 19.1.2B (01/10/2020, R): To prepare an appropriate transfer analysis a firm must: (1) assess the benefits likely to be paid and options available under the ceding arrangement; (2) compare (1) with those benefits and options available under the proposed arrangement; (3) where the proposed arrangement is a personal pension scheme, stakeholder pension scheme or defined contribution occupational pension scheme that is not a qualifying scheme, and a qualifying scheme is available to the retail client, compare the benefits and options available under the proposed arrangement with the benefits and options available under the default arrangement of the qualifying scheme; and (4) undertake the analysis in (1), (2) and (3) in accordance with COBS 19 Annex 4A and COBS 19 Annex 4C.

COBS 19.1.2C (01/10/2018, R): COBS 19.1.1-AR and COBS 19.1.2BR do not preclude a firm from preparing other forms of the analysis (for example, stochastic cashflow modelling) which are relevant to making a personal recommendation to the retail client, as long as projected outcomes at the 50th percentile are no less conservative than if the analysis had been prepared in accordance with COBS 19 Annex 4A and COBS 19 Annex 4C.

COBS 19.1.3A (01/10/2020, R): (1) To prepare a transfer value comparator, a firm must compare the transfer value offered by the ceding arrangement with the estimated value needed today to purchase the future income benefits available under the ceding arrangement using a pension annuity (calculated in accordance with COBS 19 Annex 4B and COBS 19 Annex 4C). (2) The firm must provide the transfer value comparator to the retail client in a durable medium using the format and wording in COBS 19 Annex 5 and using the notes set out in COBS 19 Annex 5 1.2R. (3) When the retail client has passed the normal retirement age of the ceding arrangement, the firm must provide a transfer value comparator applying the retirement age assumed in the calculation of the transfer value. (4) Where the ceding arrangement allows the retail client to take their benefits at an age below the scheme's normal retirement age, with no reduction for early payment and where no consent is required, then the firm must provide a transfer value comparator assuming that the retail client will retire at this age.

COBS 19.1.7C (01/10/2020, R): If a firm arranges a pension transfer, pension conversion or pension opt-out for a retail client without making a personal recommendation in relation to the pension transfer, pension conversion or pension opt-out it must: (1) make a clear record of the fact that the firm has not given that personal recommendation to the client; (1A) where the pension transfer or pension conversion is within the scope of the requirement in section 48 of the Pension Schemes Act 2015: (a) not proceed with the arrangements until it has received confirmation, from the firm that gave the advice to the retail client, that the retail client has received a personal recommendation in accordance with the requirements of COBS 19.1 (and that it was not abridged advice); and (b) if the client has received a personal recommendation, ask whether or not the recommendation was to transfer or convert; and (c) retain clear records showing evidence of (a) and (b); (1B) where the recommendation in (1A) was not to transfer or convert the retail client's subsisting rights in respect of safeguarded benefits, the firm arranging the pension transfer or pension conversion must: (a) warn the retail client that they are acting against advice not to transfer or convert; (b) ask the retail client whether they understand the consequences of acting against advice; (c) where the retail client does not understand the consequences of acting against advice, refuse to arrange the pension transfer or conversion and instead refer the retail client back to the firm that advised them not to transfer or convert for an explanation of that advice; and (d) retain a record of the communications with the retail client that evidence compliance with the requirements in (a) to (c); (2) retain the records in (1), (1A) and (1B) indefinitely.

COBS 19.1.7E (01/10/2020, R): Where the firm that has given advice to a retail client is asked by a firm arranging a pension transfer or pension conversion that is within the scope of the requirement in section 48 of the Pension Schemes Act 2015 to: (a) provide a confirmation that the retail client has received a personal recommendation in accordance with the requirements of COBS 19.1 (and that it was not abridged advice); and (b) if the client has received a personal recommendation, confirm whether or not the recommendation was to transfer or convert, the advising firm must provide the requested information to the firm arranging a pension transfer or pension conversion as soon as reasonably practicable.

COBS 19.1.9A (01/10/2020, R): Prior to finalising the firm's personal recommendation, a firm seeking evidence that the client can demonstrate their understanding of the risks in accordance with COBS 19.1.1CR(5) must: (1) make a clear record of either: (a) the evidence showing that the client demonstrated that they understood the risks involved in effecting a pension transfer or pension conversion and the steps taken by the firm to obtain that; or (b) if the firm could not obtain evidence that the client could demonstrate that understanding and the firm did not change to a recommendation not to transfer, the steps taken by the firm to obtain the evidence and clear evidence and explanation of how the firm satisfied itself on reasonable grounds that it was still suitable to continue to make the same personal recommendation; and (2) retain the records in (1) indefinitely.

PRIN 2A.2 Cross-cutting obligations

PRIN 2A.2.1 (31/07/2023, R): A firm must act in good faith towards retail customers.

PRIN 2A.2.2 (31/07/2023, R): Acting in good faith is a standard of conduct characterised by honesty, fair and open dealing and acting consistently with the reasonable expectations of retail customers.

PRIN 2A.2.5 (31/07/2023, R): If a firm identifies through complaints, its internal monitoring or from any other source, that retail customers have suffered foreseeable harm as a result of acts or omissions by the firm, it must act in good faith and take appropriate action to rectify the situation, including providing redress where appropriate.

PRIN 2A.2.6 (31/07/2023, R): PRIN 2A.2.5 does not apply where the harm identified was caused by risks inherent in a product, provided the firm reasonably believed that retail customers or the relevant retail customer (as the context requires) understood and accepted those risks.

PRIN 2A.2.8 (31/07/2023, R): A firm must avoid causing foreseeable harm to retail customers.

PRIN 2A.2.9 (31/07/2023, R): Foreseeable harm may be caused by both act and omission, in a firm's direct relationship with a retail customer or through its role in the distribution chain even where another firm in that chain also contributes to the harm.

PRIN 2A.2.14 (31/07/2023, R): A firm must enable and support retail customers to pursue their financial objectives.

PRIN 2A.2.26 (31/07/2023, R): The cross-cutting obligations (the rules in PRIN 2A.2) exhaust what is required under Principle 12.

COBS 4.2 Fair, clear and not misleading communications

COBS 4.2.1 (01/10/2018, R): (1) A firm must ensure that a communication or a financial promotion is fair, clear and not misleading. (2) This rule applies in relation to: (a) a communication by the firm to a customer in relation to designated investment business which is not MiFID, equivalent third country or optional exemption business, other than a third party prospectus; (aa) a communication to an eligible counterparty that is in relation to: (i) MiFID or equivalent third country business other than a third party prospectus; or (ii) insurance distribution; (ab) a communication by the firm to a customer in relation to MiFID, equivalent third country or optional exemption business, other than a third party prospectus; (b) a financial promotion communicated by the firm that is not: (i) an excluded communication; (ii) a non-retail communication; (iii) a third party prospectus; and (c) a financial promotion approved by the firm. (3) As part of complying with (1), a firm must take into account the nature of the client.

COBS 4.2.6 (01/04/2013, R): If, in relation to a particular communication or financial promotion, a firm takes reasonable steps to ensure it complies with the fair, clear and not misleading rule, a contravention of that rule does not give rise to a right of action under section 138D of the Act.

COBS 9.2 Assessing suitability

COBS 9.2.1 (01/10/2018, R): (1) A firm must: (a) take reasonable steps to ensure that a personal recommendation, or a decision to trade, is suitable for its client; and (b) ensure that any life policy proposed is consistent with the client's insurance demands and needs. (2) When making the personal recommendation or managing his investments, the firm must obtain the necessary information regarding the client's: (a) knowledge and experience in the investment field relevant to the specific type of designated investment or service; (b) financial situation; and (c) investment objectives; so as to enable the firm to make the recommendation, or take the decision, which is suitable for the client and for a life policy, to propose a contract that is consistent with the client's insurance demands and needs.

COBS 9.2.2 (03/01/2018, R): (1) A firm must obtain from the client such information as is necessary for the firm to understand the essential facts about him and have a reasonable basis for believing, giving due consideration to the nature and extent of the service provided, that the specific transaction to be recommended, or entered into in the course of managing: (a) meets his investment objectives; (b) is such that he is able financially to bear any related investment risks consistent with his investment objectives; and (c) is such that he has the necessary experience and knowledge in order to understand the risks involved in the transaction or in the management of his portfolio. (2) The information regarding the investment objectives of a client must include, where relevant, information on the length of time for which he wishes to hold the investment, his preferences regarding risk taking, his risk profile, and the purposes of the investment. (3) The information regarding the financial situation of a client must include, where relevant, information on the source and extent of his regular income, his assets, including liquid assets, investments and real property, and his regular financial commitments.

COBS 9.2.3 (03/01/2018, R): The information regarding a client's knowledge and experience in the investment field includes, to the extent appropriate to the nature of the client, the nature and extent of the service to be provided and the type of product or transaction envisaged, including their complexity and the risks involved, information on: (1) the types of service, transaction and designated investment with which the client is familiar; (2) the nature, volume, frequency of the client's transactions in designated investments and the period over which they have been carried out; (3) the level of education, profession or relevant former profession of the client.

COBS 9.2.4 (03/01/2018, R): A firm must not encourage a client not to provide information for the purposes of its assessment of suitability.

COBS 9.2.5 (03/01/2018, R): A firm is entitled to rely on the information provided by its clients unless it is aware that the information is manifestly out of date, inaccurate or incomplete.

COBS 9.2.6 (03/01/2018, R): If a firm does not obtain the necessary information to assess suitability, it must not make a personal recommendation to the client or take a decision to trade for him.

COBS 9.2.9 (01/11/2007, R): (1) When recommending a small friendly society life policy, a firm, for the purpose of assessing suitability, need only obtain details of the net income and expenditure of the client and his dependants. (2) A friendly society life policy is small if the premium: (a) does not exceed £50 a year; or (b) if payable weekly, £1 a week. (3) The firm must keep for five years a record of the reasons why the recommendation is considered suitable.

PTM056510 Annual allowance: money purchase annual allowance: general (HMRC Pensions Tax Manual)

General: For tax year 2015-16 and onwards, individuals who flexibly access a money purchase arrangement in certain circumstances will trigger the money purchase annual allowance rules for the tax year in which they first flexibly access their benefits and every subsequent tax year. Individuals who have flexibly accessed their benefits will, from that point onwards, be subject to a modified annual allowance test and will have a specific annual allowance in respect of their money purchase pension savings (the 'money purchase' annual allowance) for the tax year in which they first flexibly accessed and every subsequent tax year. If the money purchase annual allowance limit is exceeded for the tax year in which the individual first flexibly accessed or for any subsequent tax year, individuals will have a reduced annual allowance for the remainder of their pension savings for that tax year (in addition to the money purchase annual allowance). This reduced annual allowance is defined in the legislation as the 'alternative' annual allowance. If the money purchase annual allowance limit is not exceeded for the tax year in question individuals will retain the annual allowance for all their pension savings.

Money purchase annual allowance and alternative annual allowance - tax year 2023-24 onwards: The money purchase annual allowance for tax year 2023 onwards is £10,000. The alternative annual allowance is £30,000 or a lesser amount. It will be less than £30,000 when the tapered annual allowance also applies to the individual for the tax year concerned.

The money purchase annual allowance test: An individual who has triggered the money purchase annual allowance test for a tax year has an allowance ('money purchase' annual allowance) for money purchase pension input amounts for the tax year concerned. For tax year 2023-24 onwards, the money purchase annual allowance is £10,000. The money purchase pension input amounts which are tested against the money purchase annual allowance for the tax year concerned are those which occur (or are treated as occurring) after the individual first flexibly accesses a money purchase arrangement in certain circumstances. If the allowance for money purchase pension input amounts is exceeded, the individual has an 'alternative' annual allowance for any other pension input amounts (essentially, any pension input amounts for defined benefits arrangements) that have to be taken into account for the same tax year. To ensure that the same pension input amounts are not subject to the annual allowance twice, any pension input amounts tested against the money purchase annual allowance will not be tested against the alternative annual allowance.

Money purchase annual allowance exceeded: For the tax year 2023-24 onwards, the money purchase annual allowance is £10,000. If the individual's money purchase pension input amounts do exceed the money purchase annual allowance for the tax year concerned, the amount over the money purchase annual allowance is added to the portion (if any) of the other pension input amounts that exceeded the sum of the alternative annual allowance plus any unused annual allowance carried forward from the previous three tax years, to establish a chargeable amount potentially subject to the annual allowance charge ('the alternative chargeable amount'). The individual's total pension input amount for the tax year is also tested against the individual's available annual allowance, being the sum of the annual allowance for the tax year (or a reduced amount if the tapered annual allowance applies) and any unused annual allowance carried forward from the previous three tax years, to establish what portion (if any) is over the individual's available annual allowance ('the default chargeable amount'). If the alternative chargeable amount is greater than the default chargeable amount, the alternative chargeable amount is subject to the annual allowance charge. Otherwise the default chargeable amount (if any) is subject to the annual allowance charge.

Money purchase annual allowance not exceeded: For the tax year 2023-24 onwards, the money purchase annual allowance is £10,000. If the individual's money purchase pension input amounts do not exceed the money purchase annual allowance, the individual's total pension input amount for the tax year is tested against the individual's available annual allowance (the annual allowance or, if the tapered annual allowance applies, the reduced annual allowance for the tax year plus any unused annual allowance carried forward from the previous three tax years), and any unused money purchase annual allowance cannot be carried forward to later tax years.
4: COBS 16.6 Communications to clients - life insurance, long term care insurance and drawdown pensions. COBS 16.6.1 (01/01/2021, R): This section applies to a long-term insurer, unless, at the time of application, the client, other than an EEA ECA recipient, was habitually resident outside the United Kingdom and was not present in the United Kingdom. COBS 16.6.8R also applies to an operator of a personal pension scheme or stakeholder pension scheme in relation to a retail client who elects to make income withdrawals. COBS 16.6.2 (01/01/2016, R): The policyholder must be informed if during the term of a life policy entered into on or after 1 July 1994 there is any change in the policy conditions, the name of the insurer, its legal form or the address of its head office and, where appropriate, of the agency or branch which concluded the contract, and certain Solvency II Directive information in the event of a change in the policy conditions or amendment of the applicable law. Notification must be made in a clear and accurate manner, in writing, and in an official language of the State of commitment or another permitted language. COBS 16.6.3 (01/01/2016, R): If a life policy entered into on or after 1 July 1994 provides for the payment of bonuses and the amounts are unspecified, the long-term insurer must, in every calendar year except the first, either notify the policyholder in writing of the amount of any bonus that has become payable and not previously notified, or give the policyholder sufficient information in writing to determine that amount. COBS 16.6.3A (01/01/2016, R): If a firm provides figures, on or after 1 January 2016, about the potential future development of bonuses under a with-profits policy, it must inform the policyholder annually in writing of any differences between actual bonuses payable to date and the figures previously provided. COBS 16.6.4 (01/11/2007, R): When a firm provides information under this section, it must provide it in a durable medium, unless the contract is made by telephone, in which case the firm may give the information orally, and if the customer enters into the contract, a written version must be sent within five business days. COBS 16.6.5 (01/11/2007, R): Where a life policy is effected jointly, the information required by this section may be sent to the first named client. COBS 16.6.6 (01/11/2007, R): A firm must make an adequate record of information provided to a customer under this section and retain that record for a minimum of five years after the information is provided. COBS 16.6.7 (01/11/2007, R): At each anniversary of the date on which a long-term care insurance contract based on single premium investment bonds was entered into, the insurer must provide the retail client with a table containing at least the current fund value and projected future policy values, inform the client if future policy values may be insufficient to fulfil the original purpose of the contract, and inform the client how to obtain advice on investments in respect of long-term care insurance contracts and that it is in their best interest to do so. COBS 16.6.7A (01/02/2021, R): Defines terms used in the rest of COBS 16.6: 'annual statement' is the information required to be provided annually under COBS 16.6.8R; 'cash terms' means pounds and pence; 'cash-like investments' includes cash or near cash and units in qualifying money market funds; 'drawdown fund' means a capped drawdown pension fund or flexi-access drawdown pension fund; a retail client is a 'non-advised retail client' if the firm has not determined on reasonable grounds that the client received a personal recommendation on investing the sums or assets in their drawdown fund. COBS 16.6.8 (01/02/2021, R): At intervals of no longer than 12 months, beginning on the date a retail client first takes a pension commencement lump sum or uncrystallised funds pension lump sum payment, or first makes an income withdrawal, the relevant operator of a personal pension scheme or stakeholder pension scheme must provide the retail client with information necessary to review the decision, and inform the client that if their circumstances or retirement objectives have changed it may be in their best interests to review their choice of pension product, review their investment choices, take regulated advice to understand their options at retirement, and seek out guidance. COBS 16.6.8A (01/02/2021, R): If a retail client is invested in a pathway investment, the annual statement must include a short description of each pathway investment held including the corresponding investment pathway option and current value in cash terms, how the drawdown fund is split across pathway investments if invested in two or more, a short description of pathway investment options not currently invested in, and a statement reminding the client that they can at any time select a different pathway option, select a non-pathway investment, split their drawdown fund across multiple pathway investments where available, choose a different product to access their pension savings, or shop around. COBS 16.6.10 (06/04/2026, R): The annual statement must include costs and charges information based on actual costs and charges, including transaction costs and the cost of advice, charged by the operator or other parties and paid out of the retail client's drawdown fund or the personal pension scheme or stakeholder pension scheme from which an uncrystallised funds pension lump sum was paid, aggregated, totalled, and expressed in pounds and pence. Where the scheme is in partial drawdown, the operator may include costs and charges for the whole scheme but must make clear whether the figures relate to the whole scheme or only the drawdown fund. If the operator lacks the necessary information it must take all reasonable steps to obtain it, and if exact figures remain unavailable despite reasonable steps it must provide a reasonable estimate or, if that is not possible, a written statement explaining which costs and charges are not included. The operator must include a written statement disclosing whether any adviser remuneration, including adviser charges, consultancy charges, charges for a targeted support service, commission or commission equivalent, is included in the aggregated figure, and must make clear what period the costs and charges information covers. COBS 16.6.11 (01/02/2021, R): COBS 16.6.10R does not apply where costs and charges are discharged by payment of the fixed price of a drawdown pension product, which has been clearly disclosed to the retail client.
5: MCOB 11.6 Responsible lending and financing. MCOB 11.6.2 (21/03/2016, R): Except as provided in MCOB 11.6.3R, MCOB 11.6.57R (interest roll-up mortgages) and MCOB 11.7 (transitional arrangements), before entering into, or agreeing to vary, a regulated mortgage contract or home purchase plan, a firm must assess whether the customer (and any guarantor) will be able to pay the sums due, and must not enter into the transaction unless it can demonstrate the new or varied contract is affordable for the customer (and any guarantor). References to payment of sums due mean, for a regulated mortgage contract, the making of payments to repay the sums advanced and interest reasonably expected to accrue, and for a home purchase plan, payment of the sums due under the plan, in each case as they fall due. References to the customer must be read as referring also to any guarantor where the context permits. MCOB 11.6.3 (22/07/2025, R): MCOB 11.6.2R does not apply to entering into a new regulated mortgage contract or home purchase plan as a replacement for an existing one between the customer and the firm, whether or not the new contract relates to the same property, including where the original lender is not entering into contracts with new customers and is in the same group as the new lender, or to a variation of an existing contract or plan, provided the proposed new or varied contract does not involve the customer taking on additional borrowing beyond the amount currently outstanding (other than to finance a product or arrangement fee) and there is no change to the terms likely to be material to affordability. MCOB 11.6.2R also does not apply to a variation that reduces (including to zero) capital repayments under a repayment mortgage for no longer than six months, reverses a term extension within six months of it taking effect, or is made solely for forbearance where the customer has or is avoiding a payment shortfall, subject to conditions that the contract remains a repayment mortgage, has not previously been varied in reliance on the same paragraph, and is not a bridging loan or second charge contract. MCOB 11.6.2R also does not apply to a variation reducing the term of a contract, though the firm must still consider affordability in line with Principle 12 (Consumer Duty), PRIN 2A and its responsible lending policy. MCOB 11.6.5 (21/03/2016, R): When assessing affordability under MCOB 11.6.2R, a firm must not base its assessment on the equity in the property used as security or take account of expected increases in property prices, must take full account of the customer's income net of income tax and national insurance and, as a minimum, the customer's committed expenditure and the basic essential expenditure and basic quality-of-living costs of the household, must (if a mortgage lender) assess affordability on the basis of both capital repayment and interest payment over the term except where lending under an interest-only mortgage in accordance with MCOB 11.6.41R(1), and must (if a mortgage lender) take account of the impact of likely future interest rate increases as set out in MCOB 11.6.18R. MCOB 11.6.6 (26/04/2014, R): For the purposes of MCOB 11.6.2R, a firm must not rely on a general declaration of affordability by the customer or their representative. MCOB 11.6.8 (26/04/2014, R): In taking account of the customer's income under MCOB 11.6.5R(2)(a), a firm must obtain evidence of the income declared by the customer for the application, of a type and period adequate to support each element of income taken into account and subject to appropriate anti-fraud controls, and must not accept self-certification of income, with the evidence's source independent of the customer. MCOB 11.6.10 (26/04/2014, R): For the purposes of the affordability assessment, committed expenditure under MCOB 11.6.5R(2)(b)(i) is the customer's credit and other contractual commitments continuing after the contract or variation is entered into; basic essential expenditure under MCOB 11.6.5R(2)(b)(ii) comprises housekeeping, gas, electricity and other heating, water, telephone, council tax, buildings insurance, ground rent and service charge for leasehold properties, and essential travel including to work or school; basic quality-of-living costs under the same provision are household expenditure that is hard to reduce and gives a basic quality of life beyond the essential expenditure. MCOB 11.6.12 (26/04/2014, R): A firm may generally rely on evidence of income or expenditure information provided by the customer unless it has reason to doubt it, must take reasonable steps to obtain details of the customer's actual outstanding commitments for committed expenditure, and for basic essential expenditure and basic quality-of-living costs may obtain actual expenditure details or use statistical or modelled data appropriate to the household composition, applying realistic assumptions if modelled data is used. MCOB 11.6.14 (26/04/2014, R): If a firm is, or should reasonably be, aware that there will likely be future changes to the customer's income and expenditure during the contract term, it must take them into account when assessing affordability under MCOB 11.6.2R. MCOB 11.6.16 (21/03/2016, R): Where a purpose of the contract or variation is debt consolidation and, for a first charge contract, the customer is credit-impaired, and if the debts to be repaid using the sums raised would otherwise render the transaction unaffordable, the firm must take reasonable steps to ensure those debts are actually repaid on completion, unless the firm has instead assumed the debts will not be repaid and included them as committed expenditure in the assessment. MCOB 11.6.18 (02/05/2014, R): In taking account of likely future interest rate increases under MCOB 11.6.5R(4), a mortgage lender must consider likely future interest rates over a minimum of five years from the expected start of the term, unless the rate is fixed for five years or more (or for the duration if shorter), having regard to market expectations and any prevailing Financial Policy Committee recommendation on interest-rate stress tests and being able to justify the basis used; even if that basis indicates rates are likely to fall or rise by less than 1% over the first five years, the lender must assume a minimum 1% rise over that period. MCOB 11.6.18A (21/03/2016, R): A second charge lender must also consider, under MCOB 11.6.5R(4), the likely future interest rates of any existing regulated mortgage contract that will remain in existence after the new second charge contract is entered into, basing the assessment at minimum on the outstanding balance of that existing contract. MCOB 11.6.20 (21/03/2016, R): A firm must put in place and operate a written responsible lending or financing policy, approved by its governing body, addressing how income and expenditure are assessed (acceptable income types and proportions, treatment of income variation, acceptable evidence, and treatment of committed expenditure and essential/quality-of-living costs), how future interest rates are factored in, the calculations used to determine affordability, how anti-fraud controls are incorporated, how the method for calculating advance size is monitored including review timing and KPIs, the actions to be taken if that method underperforms, how regular compliance audits are conducted, how record-keeping requirements under MCOB 11.6.60R are met, interest-only policy matters under MCOB 11.6.50R where applicable, and how MCOB 11.7 transitional exceptions are applied including use of management information to monitor those exceptions where applicable. MCOB 11.6.21A (21/03/2016, R): An MCD mortgage lender must keep a record of the valuation and types of immovable property accepted as security, and of the related mortgage underwriting policies used. MCOB 11.6.22 (26/04/2014, R): A firm must put in place, and be able to demonstrate, robust systems and controls including management information and KPIs to monitor the effectiveness of its affordability assessments, including in preventing payment difficulties. MCOB 11.6.24 (26/04/2014, R): A firm must ensure compliance with its responsible lending or financing policy is reviewed at least once per calendar year, by its internal audit function (or outsourced equivalent) if it has one, or otherwise by its internal compliance function (or outsourced equivalent). MCOB 11.6.25 (26/04/2014, R): Where a regulated mortgage contract is solely for a business purpose, a firm may opt to apply MCOB 11.6.26R to MCOB 11.6.31R in place of MCOB 11.6.5R to MCOB 11.6.19G. MCOB 11.6.26 (26/04/2014, R): When assessing affordability for a business-purpose contract, a firm must not base its assessment on the equity in the property or expected property price increases; where repayments are made from the customer's own resources, must take full account of the customer's income net of tax and national insurance, or net assets, or both, and the customer's committed expenditure, and take account in general terms of basic essential expenditure and basic quality-of-living costs; where repayments are made from the business's financial resources, must take full account of the strength of those resources; if the customer relies on the business for personal income, must at minimum consider in general terms whether the business can support the customer's basic essential and quality-of-living costs; must assess affordability on the basis of both capital repayment and interest payment over the term except where lending under an interest-only mortgage in accordance with MCOB 11.6.41R(1); and must take account of the impact of likely future interest rate increases. MCOB 11.6.27 (26/04/2014, R): For the purposes of MCOB 11.6.2R, a firm must not rely on a general declaration of affordability by the customer or their representative. MCOB 11.6.28 (26/04/2014, R): In taking account of the customer's income or net assets and the business's resources under MCOB 11.6.26R(2), a firm must obtain evidence of the income or net assets and business resources as declared by the customer for the application, and must not accept self-certification of income, with the evidence's source independent of the customer. MCOB 11.6.29 (26/04/2014, R): In MCOB 11.6.26R, the meaning of committed expenditure and basic essential and quality-of-living costs is as set out in MCOB 11.6.10R. MCOB 11.6.31 (26/04/2014, R): If a firm is, or should reasonably be, aware that there will likely be future changes to the customer's income and expenditure, or the business's resources, during the contract term, it must take them into account when assessing affordability under MCOB 11.6.2R. 6: HMRC Inheritance Tax: thresholds, rules and allowances (gov.uk). There is normally no Inheritance Tax to pay if the estate's value is below the £325,000 threshold, or if everything above that threshold is left to a spouse, civil partner, charity or community amateur sports club; the estate's value may still need to be reported even if below the threshold. If a home is given away to children (including adopted, foster or stepchildren) or grandchildren, the threshold can increase to £500,000, provided the estate is worth less than £2 million. If married or in a civil partnership and the estate is worth less than the available threshold, any unused threshold can be transferred to the partner's threshold on death. The standard Inheritance Tax rate is 40%, charged only on the part of the estate above the threshold; for example, an estate worth £500,000 against a £325,000 threshold is taxed at 40% of £175,000. A reduced rate of 36% applies on some assets if 10% or more of the estate's net value (total value minus debts) is left to charity in the will. Reliefs such as Business Relief or Agricultural Relief can allow some assets to pass free of Inheritance Tax or with a reduced bill, and taper relief may reduce the tax charged on lifetime gifts depending on when they were given. Inheritance Tax owed is paid from the estate's funds to HMRC, normally by the executor; beneficiaries do not normally pay tax on what they inherit, though related taxes such as tax on rental income may apply. People who receive gifts may have to pay Inheritance Tax themselves only if the giver gave away more than £325,000 and died within 7 years. A home can be passed to a spouse or civil partner on death with no Inheritance Tax to pay; left to another person, it counts towards the estate's value. The £500,000 threshold uplift for passing on a home applies where the home (or a share in it) is left to children or grandchildren and the estate is worth less than £2 million. If a home is given away before death, there is normally no Inheritance Tax to pay if the giver moves out and lives for a further 7 years; continuing to live in the property requires paying rent at the going local rate and a share of the bills, otherwise it counts as a gift with reservation (a gift from which the giver continues to benefit) and is added back to the estate's value on death, unless only part of the property was given away and the new owners also live there, in which case no rent is required. If death occurs within 7 years of giving away all or part of a property, the home is treated as a gift and the 7 year rule applies, though the 7 year rule does not apply to gifts with reservation. On gifts generally, Inheritance Tax may be due after death depending on who received the gift and their relationship to the giver, the gift's value, and when it was given. Gifts include money, household and personal goods, a house, land or buildings, stocks and shares listed on the London Stock Exchange, and unlisted shares held for less than 2 years before death; selling something for less than its market value also creates a gift equal to the difference in value. Anything left in a will is not a gift but forms part of the estate. There is no Inheritance Tax on gifts between spouses or civil partners who live permanently in the UK and are legally married or in a civil partnership, nor on gifts to charities or political parties. Each tax year, an annual exemption allows giving away up to £3,000 worth of gifts, to one person or split between several, free of Inheritance Tax, with any unused annual exemption carried forward for one further tax year only; the tax year runs from 6 April to 5 April. A small gift allowance permits gifts of up to £250 per person each tax year, as long as no other allowance has been used on that same person, and birthday or Christmas gifts from regular income are exempt. Wedding or civil partnership gifts are tax free up to £5,000 to a child, £2,500 to a grandchild or great-grandchild, and £1,000 to any other person, and this allowance can be combined with any other allowance except the small gift allowance. Regular payments made from surplus regular income to help with another person's living costs ('normal expenditure out of income') are tax free with no upper limit, provided the giver can still afford their own usual living costs after the payments, and this can be combined with any other allowance except the small gift allowance. Under the 7 year rule, no Inheritance Tax is due on gifts if the giver survives 7 years after giving them, unless the gift was made into a trust; gifts given in the 3 years before death are taxed at the full 40% rate, and gifts given 3 to 7 years before death are taxed on a sliding taper relief scale (32% in year 3 to 4, 24% in year 4 to 5, 16% in year 5 to 6, 8% in year 6 to 7, 0% from 7 years), which only applies where total gifts in the 7 years before death exceed the £325,000 threshold. A gift with reservation, such as giving away a home but continuing to live there, a caravan but still using it for holidays, or a painting but still displaying it, counts towards the estate's value regardless of when it was given. Inheritance Tax on gifts is normally paid by the estate, unless the giver gave away more than £325,000 in the 7 years before death, in which case recipients of gifts within that period become liable to pay the tax on their own gifts. For deaths outside the UK, Inheritance Tax is only paid on UK assets such as UK property or bank accounts; HMRC treats a person as based abroad if they lived in the UK for less than 10 years in the last 20 years, and certain assets such as foreign currency accounts, overseas pensions, and holdings in authorised unit trusts or open-ended investment companies are excluded from Inheritance Tax, with different rules for trust assets, government gilts, and visiting armed forces members. For deaths on or before 5 April 2025, a person who died was treated as UK-based if their permanent home (domicile) was in the UK, they lived in the UK for 15 of the last 20 years, or they had their permanent home in the UK at any time in the last 3 years of their life; a double-taxation treaty may allow the executor to reclaim tax if the same assets are taxed by both the UK and the country where the deceased lived. COBS 9.2 Assessing suitability. COBS 9.2.1 (01/10/2018, R): A firm must take reasonable steps to ensure that a personal recommendation, or a decision to trade, is suitable for its client, and must ensure that any life policy proposed is consistent with the client's insurance demands and needs. When making the personal recommendation or managing investments, the firm must obtain the necessary information regarding the client's knowledge and experience in the investment field relevant to the specific type of designated investment or service, financial situation, and investment objectives, so as to enable the firm to make a suitable recommendation or decision, and for a life policy, to propose a contract consistent with the client's insurance demands and needs. COBS 9.2.2 (03/01/2018, R): A firm must obtain from the client such information as is necessary to understand the essential facts about them and have a reasonable basis for believing, given the nature and extent of the service provided, that the specific transaction recommended or entered into in the course of managing meets the client's investment objectives, is one the client is able financially to bear the related investment risks of consistent with their investment objectives, and is one the client has the necessary experience and knowledge to understand the risks of, including in relation to managing their portfolio. Information on investment objectives must include, where relevant, the length of time the client wishes to hold the investment, their risk preferences and risk profile, and the purposes of the investment. Information on financial situation must include, where relevant, the source and extent of regular income, assets including liquid assets, investments and real property, and regular financial commitments. COBS 9.2.3 (03/01/2018, R): Information on a client's knowledge and experience in the investment field includes, to the extent appropriate to the nature of the client, the service to be provided, and the type of product or transaction envisaged including its complexity and risks, information on the types of service, transaction and designated investment the client is familiar with, the nature, volume and frequency of the client's transactions in designated investments and the period over which they were carried out, and the client's level of education, profession or relevant former profession. COBS 9.2.4 (03/01/2018, R): A firm must not encourage a client not to provide information for the purposes of its suitability assessment. COBS 9.2.5 (03/01/2018, R): A firm is entitled to rely on information provided by its clients unless it is aware the information is manifestly out of date, inaccurate or incomplete. COBS 9.2.6 (03/01/2018, R): If a firm does not obtain the necessary information to assess suitability, it must not make a personal recommendation to the client or take a decision to trade for them. COBS 9.2.9 (01/11/2007, R): When recommending a small friendly society life policy, a firm need only obtain, for suitability purposes, details of the net income and expenditure of the client and their dependants; such a policy is small if the premium does not exceed £50 a year or £1 a week if paid weekly; the firm must keep a record for five years of the reasons why the recommendation is considered suitable.
7: MCOB 8 Equity release: advising and selling standards. MCOB 8.1.1 (31/10/2004, R): This chapter applies to a firm in a category listed in the MCOB 8.1.2R table, in accordance with that table. MCOB 8.1.2A (26/04/2014, R): MCOB 8.6A only applies to an equity release provider in relation to entering into an equity release transaction where no firm is arranging the transaction to whom MCOB 8.6A would otherwise apply. MCOB 8.3.2B (26/04/2014, R): For the purposes of MCOB 4.4A.2R(1) there is one relevant market for equity release transactions; a firm offering only lifetime mortgages or only home reversion plans must disclose under MCOB 4.4A.1R(1) that it is limited in that regard in the range of products it can offer. MCOB 8.3.3 (26/04/2014, R): For additional disclosure for distance mortgage mediation contracts, MCOB 4.5's reference to MCOB 4 is read as MCOB 4 as modified by MCOB 8. MCOB 8.3.4 (26/04/2014, R): For advised sales, MCOB 4.7A is replaced by MCOB 8.5A; for execution-only sales, MCOB 4.8A is replaced by MCOB 8.6A. MCOB 8.5A.2 (26/04/2014, R): If a firm advises a particular customer to enter into an equity release transaction, or to vary an existing one, it must take reasonable steps to ensure the transaction is, or after variation will be, suitable for that customer. MCOB 8.5A.3 (26/04/2014, R): A reference to advice to enter into an equity release transaction includes advice to vary an existing one. MCOB 8.5A.5 (26/04/2014, R): An equity release transaction is not suitable unless it is appropriate to the customer's needs and circumstances; a firm must base that determination on facts disclosed by the customer and other relevant facts it is or should reasonably be aware of; no advice to enter into a transaction must be given if no transaction in the firm's product range is suitable; if a mortgage lender is dealing with an existing customer with a payment shortfall and has concluded no transaction satisfies MCOB 8.5A.2R, the firm must nonetheless have regard to MCOB 13.3. MCOB 8.5A.6 (26/04/2014, R): In assessing appropriateness under MCOB 8.5A.5R, a firm must consider whether the benefits outweigh any adverse effect on the customer's entitlement to means-tested benefits and on their tax position (such as loss of an Age Allowance); alternative methods of raising funds such as a local authority or other grant, a further advance under an existing or new regulated mortgage contract, or an additional release under an existing home reversion plan; whether the customer's requirements fall within the provider's known eligibility criteria; the customer's preferences for their estate; the customer's health and life expectancy; the customer's future plans and needs; whether the customer prefers or needs stability in payment amounts given the impact of future interest rate changes; any other feature preferences or needs; and, for lifetime mortgages only, whether it is more appropriate to pay fees up front rather than add them to the sum advanced. MCOB 8.5A.8 (26/04/2014, R): Where a firm has insufficient knowledge of means-tested benefits and tax allowances to reach a conclusion on the MCOB 8.5A.6R(1) factor, it must refer the customer to an appropriate source such as the Pension Service, HMRC or Citizens Advice (or similar) to establish the required information. MCOB 8.5A.10 (26/04/2014, R): If a customer declines to seek further information on means-tested benefits, tax allowances or local authority grants, or rejects the firm's conclusion that alternative funding methods are more suitable, a firm can still advise the customer to enter into a suitable equity release transaction, but must confirm the basis of the advice to the customer in a durable medium. MCOB 8.5A.11 (26/04/2014, R): Where the main purpose of an equity release transaction is debt consolidation, in assessing suitability under MCOB 8.5A.5R(1) a firm must also take account of the costs of increasing the repayment period, whether it is appropriate to secure a previously unsecured loan, and, where the customer has known payment difficulties, whether negotiating an arrangement with creditors would be more appropriate than equity release. MCOB 8.5A.15 (26/04/2014, R): When advising on suitability, a firm must explain to the customer that the appropriateness assessment is based on their current circumstances, which may change in future. MCOB 8.5A.19 (26/04/2014, R): A firm must make and retain a record of the customer information obtained for MCOB 8.5A purposes including needs, circumstances and apparent satisfaction of eligibility criteria; an explanation of why any advice given complies with MCOB 8.5A.2R and MCOB 8.5A.5R(1); any advice rejected by the customer including reasons and the transaction proceeded with as an execution-only sale; and, where applicable, the customer's positive choice under MCOB 4.6A.2R; these records must be retained for a minimum of three years from the date advice was given, or for (d), from the date the choice was made. MCOB 8.6A.9 (26/04/2014, R): Whenever a firm enters into or arranges an execution-only sale it must make and maintain a record of the required information satisfying MCOB 8.6A.4R(2), the durable-medium information under MCOB 8.6A.4R(3), the customer's confirmation under MCOB 8.6A.4R(4) where applicable, and any rejected advice with reasons; this record must be retained for a minimum of three years from the date the transaction was entered into or arranged. MCOB 8.6A.10 (26/04/2014, R): The restrictions on execution-only sales in MCOB 8.6A do not apply to a variation made solely for forbearance where the customer has, or is avoiding, a payment shortfall. 8: COBS 9.2 Assessing suitability. COBS 9.2.1 (01/10/2018, R): A firm must take reasonable steps to ensure that a personal recommendation, or a decision to trade, is suitable for its client, and must ensure that any life policy proposed is consistent with the client's insurance demands and needs. When making the personal recommendation or managing investments, the firm must obtain the necessary information regarding the client's knowledge and experience in the investment field relevant to the specific type of designated investment or service, financial situation, and investment objectives, so as to enable the firm to make a suitable recommendation or decision, and for a life policy, to propose a contract consistent with the client's insurance demands and needs. COBS 9.2.2 (03/01/2018, R): A firm must obtain from the client such information as is necessary to understand the essential facts about them and have a reasonable basis for believing, given the nature and extent of the service provided, that the specific transaction recommended or entered into in the course of managing meets the client's investment objectives, is one the client is able financially to bear the related investment risks of consistent with their investment objectives, and is one the client has the necessary experience and knowledge to understand the risks of, including in relation to managing their portfolio. Information on investment objectives must include, where relevant, the length of time the client wishes to hold the investment, their risk preferences and risk profile, and the purposes of the investment. Information on financial situation must include, where relevant, the source and extent of regular income, assets including liquid assets, investments and real property, and regular financial commitments. COBS 9.2.3 (03/01/2018, R): Information on a client's knowledge and experience in the investment field includes, to the extent appropriate to the nature of the client, the service to be provided, and the type of product or transaction envisaged including its complexity and risks, information on the types of service, transaction and designated investment the client is familiar with, the nature, volume and frequency of the client's transactions in designated investments and the period over which they were carried out, and the client's level of education, profession or relevant former profession. COBS 9.2.4 (03/01/2018, R): A firm must not encourage a client not to provide information for the purposes of its suitability assessment. COBS 9.2.5 (03/01/2018, R): A firm is entitled to rely on information provided by its clients unless it is aware the information is manifestly out of date, inaccurate or incomplete. COBS 9.2.6 (03/01/2018, R): If a firm does not obtain the necessary information to assess suitability, it must not make a personal recommendation to the client or take a decision to trade for them. COBS 9.2.9 (01/11/2007, R): When recommending a small friendly society life policy, a firm need only obtain, for suitability purposes, details of the net income and expenditure of the client and their dependants; such a policy is small if the premium does not exceed £50 a year or £1 a week if paid weekly; the firm must keep a record for five years of the reasons why the recommendation is considered suitable. COBS 4.2 Fair, clear and not misleading communications. COBS 4.2.1 (01/10/2018, R): A firm must ensure that a communication or a financial promotion is fair, clear and not misleading. This rule applies to a communication by the firm to a customer in relation to designated investment business which is not MiFID, equivalent third country or optional exemption business, other than a third party prospectus; a communication to an eligible counterparty relating to MiFID or equivalent third country business (other than a third party prospectus) or to insurance distribution; a communication by the firm to a customer relating to MiFID, equivalent third country or optional exemption business, other than a third party prospectus; a financial promotion communicated by the firm that is not an excluded communication, a non-retail communication, or a third party prospectus; and a financial promotion approved by the firm. As part of complying with this rule, a firm must take into account the nature of the client. COBS 4.2.6 (01/04/2013, R): If, in relation to a particular communication or financial promotion, a firm takes reasonable steps to ensure it complies with the fair, clear and not misleading rule, a contravention of that rule does not give rise to a right of action for damages under section 138D of the Act.
9: Pensions Act 2008, Part 1: automatic enrolment (sections 3, 7, 8). Section 3, Automatic enrolment: this section applies to a jobholder who is aged at least 22, who has not reached pensionable age, and to whom earnings of more than £10,000 are payable by the employer in the relevant pay reference period. The employer must make prescribed arrangements by which the jobholder becomes an active member of an automatic enrolment scheme with effect from the automatic enrolment date. This duty does not apply if the jobholder was already an active member of a qualifying scheme on the automatic enrolment date, or if, within the prescribed period before that date, the jobholder ceased to be an active member of a qualifying scheme because of their own action or omission. Regulations may require information about the arrangements to be provided by the employer or, for an occupational pension scheme, its trustees or managers, or, for a personal pension scheme, its provider; for a personal pension scheme, regulations may also deem an agreement to exist between the jobholder and the provider for the jobholder to become an active member on terms determined by regulations. For a pay reference period of more or less than 12 months, the £10,000 earnings threshold applies proportionately more or less. The automatic enrolment date is the first day this section applies to the person as a jobholder of the employer, subject to section 4. References elsewhere in this Part to an automatic enrolment scheme mean a pension scheme that is an automatic enrolment scheme in relation to that jobholder. Section 7, Jobholder's right to opt in: this section applies to a jobholder who is not an active member of a qualifying scheme, except at a time when arrangements are already required to be made under section 3 or 5 in respect of that jobholder. The jobholder may give notice requiring the employer to arrange for them to become an active member of an automatic enrolment scheme. The Secretary of State may make regulations about the form and content of the notice, the arrangements the employer must make, and the date from which the jobholder becomes an active member; regulations may require information to be provided by the employer or, for an occupational pension scheme, its trustees or managers, or, for a personal pension scheme, its provider, and may deem an agreement to exist between the jobholder and a personal pension scheme provider on terms determined by regulations. If a jobholder becomes an active member following a section 7 notice and, within 12 months of that notice, ceases to be an active member and gives a further section 7 notice, that further notice does not require the employer to arrange active membership again, but any arrangements the employer does make for the jobholder to become an active member within that 12-month period must still be made in accordance with the regulations under this section. Section 8, Jobholder's right to opt out: this section applies whenever arrangements under section 3(2), 5(2) or 7(3) apply to a jobholder to become an active member of an automatic enrolment scheme. If the jobholder gives notice under this section, they are treated for all purposes as not having become an active member of the scheme on that occasion, and any contributions paid by the jobholder or by the employer on their behalf on the basis of that membership must be refunded in accordance with prescribed requirements; regulations under this provision may address the time within which contributions must be refunded, how the refund amount is calculated, and the refund procedure. The Secretary of State may make further regulations about opt-out notices covering their form and content, the period within which a notice must be given, the person to whom it must be given, requirements for arrangements enabling notices to be given, and required actions in consequence of a notice; the regulations must in any case require the notice to include information about the effect of giving it and to be signed or otherwise authorised by the jobholder. COBS 19.6 Restriction on charges in qualifying schemes. COBS 19.6.1 (06/04/2015, R): This section applies to an operator of a qualifying scheme. COBS 19.6.2 (06/04/2015, R): The administration charge restrictions in COBS 19.6.4R do not apply to a default arrangement under which, at any time before benefits come into payment, the benefits accruing to the member involve, or involve an option to have, a promise by or to be obtained from a third party about the rate or amount of those benefits. COBS 19.6.4 (06/04/2015, R): For a default arrangement within a qualifying scheme, a firm may only make, impose or facilitate payment of an administration charge by way of an accrued rights charge or a combination charge structure if the limits in COBS 19.6.6R are not exceeded, or if the firm has obtained appropriate express agreement to exceed the limits, where that agreement contains the member's acknowledgement that the charge is likely to exceed the limits, giving the agreement is not a condition of becoming or remaining a scheme member, and the agreement has not been given for services the operator must provide under the regulatory system or general law, or which are core services. COBS 19.6.6 (06/04/2015, R): The administration charge limits are, for a qualifying scheme using only an accrued rights charge, 0.75% of the value of the accrued rights; for a qualifying scheme using a combination charge structure, a flat-fee element of £25 annually, a contribution percentage element of 2.5% of contributions annually, and an associated accrued rights charge element set at the rates in the COBS 19.6.7R table. COBS 19.6.9 (06/04/2016, R): A firm must not make any administration charge, or otherwise make or facilitate any payment or provide any non-monetary benefit, in respect of a service provided by a third party in connection with a qualifying scheme, where doing so would decrease the value of the accrued rights of any scheme member, unless the firm has obtained express agreement from the relevant member to that payment. 10: FCA Policy Statement PS23/6, Financial promotion rules for cryptoassets (8 June 2023). In January 2022, the Government published a consultation response setting out its intention to legislate to bring certain promotions of qualifying cryptoassets within the FCA's remit; the proposed legislative approach was updated in a policy statement published 1 February 2023. The financial promotions regime applies to all firms marketing cryptoassets to UK consumers, regardless of whether the firm is based overseas or what technology is used to make the promotion. The FCA had earlier consulted on financial promotion rules for high-risk investments including cryptoassets (CP22/2) and, in August 2022, published final rules for other high-risk investments excluding cryptoassets (PS22/10), having noted it would make cryptoasset-specific rules once the relevant legislation was made and intended a consistent approach to cryptoassets and other high-risk investments. PS23/6 summarises feedback received on CP22/2 and sets out the FCA's final policy position and near final Handbook rules; having considered that feedback, the FCA proceeded with categorising cryptoassets as Restricted Mass Market Investments and applying the associated restrictions on how they may be marketed to UK consumers, making targeted changes to the consultation proposals to align with the rules set out in PS22/10 for other high-risk investments. The FCA also published a Guidance Consultation (GC23/1) on non-Handbook guidance concerning the requirement that financial promotions be fair, clear and not misleading. The work was framed as more urgent given that cryptoasset prices had fallen sharply, around 75% between November 2021 and June 2022, and several firm failures had caused significant consumer losses, often involving misleading promotions offering high rates of return with no evidence of how these could be achieved, and promoting high-risk, complex products as 'stable', such as the algorithmic stablecoin project Terra/Luna. Even once the financial promotions regime took effect, cryptoassets remained high risk and largely unregulated; consumers were advised to invest only if they understood the risks involved and were prepared to lose all their money, and not to expect protection from the Financial Services Compensation Scheme or the Financial Ombudsman Service if something went wrong. The near final rules were set out in Appendix 1 to PS23/6, published as near final immediately after the relevant legislation was made to give firms maximum preparation time; the FCA Board approved the rules as near final, with no further changes expected absent exceptional circumstances, and the FCA expected the rules to have effect from 8 October 2023. The FCA stated it would take robust action against firms breaching these requirements, which could include requesting takedowns of breaching websites, placing firms on its warning list, imposing restrictions to prevent harmful promotions, and enforcement action; firms illegally communicating financial promotions to UK consumers would be committing a criminal offence punishable by an unlimited fine, up to 2 years' imprisonment, or both. In the original CP22/2 consultation, the proposed restrictions accompanying the Restricted Mass Market Investments classification, in addition to the overarching requirement that financial promotions be fair, clear and not misleading, included clear risk warnings, a ban on incentives to invest, positive frictions, client categorisation requirements, and appropriateness assessments. Regulatory status note (pending reform, as of June 2026): the FCA is in the process of building a more comprehensive cryptoasset regulatory regime under its Crypto Roadmap, following the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) Regulations 2026 made by Parliament on 4 February 2026, with the new regime expected to take effect 25 October 2027. As part of this roadmap, the FCA published CP25/25 (17 September 2025), consulting on how existing FCA Handbook rules, including COBS, would apply to firms conducting newly regulated cryptoasset activities; that consultation has since closed. The FCA subsequently published CP26/4 (23 January 2026), 'Application of FCA Handbook for regulated cryptoasset activities – part 2', a follow-up consultation addressing Consumer Duty, redress and dispute resolution, COBS, credit for crypto purchases, training and competence, the Senior Managers and Certification Regime, regulatory reporting, and cryptoasset safeguarding, among other topics; responses to CP26/4 closed 12 March 2026. The financial promotion rules in PS23/6 remain in force as the current regime, but firms and researchers should be aware that the broader cryptoasset conduct-of-business framework is under active consultation and subject to change before the new regime's 25 October 2027 commencement.
